title: Implement animal health and bio-security programs

lessons.title: Why animal health and bio-security matter
lessons.html:
Prevention is cheaper than cure

A single disease outbreak can wipe out a year's profit. Foot-and-mouth disease can close a whole area to cattle sales, avian influenza can force a poultry farm to cull its flock, and diseases like brucellosis and tuberculosis also infect people. An animal health program keeps animals healthy through planned vaccination, parasite control and good management. A bio-security program keeps disease out of the farm and stops it spreading inside the farm.

How disease enters and spreads

  • New animals – bought-in stock, rams and bulls are the most common way disease arrives.
  • People and vehicles – visitors, stock trucks, feed lorries and contractors carry germs on boots, clothes and tyres.
  • Wildlife, birds and rodents – wild birds near poultry, kudu and buffalo near cattle, rats in feed stores.
  • Feed and water – contaminated feed, dirty troughs and shared water points.
  • Equipment – shared needles, dehorners, castration tools and trailers.

The law

The Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 controls animal diseases in South Africa. Some diseases are controlled or notifiable: if you suspect one, you must report it to the state veterinarian. Examples include foot-and-mouth disease, anthrax, avian influenza and African swine fever. Never move or sell animals from a herd you suspect is infected until the state vet has given instructions. Stock remedies must be used according to Act 36 of 1947 and the label.

As a supervisor at NQF level 4 your role is to put the farm's program into practice: make sure the right things happen on the right day, records are kept and problems are reported quickly.

lessons.title: Running the animal health program
lessons.html:
The health calendar

Most farms have a health calendar drawn up with their vet. It lists vaccinations, dipping or pour-on treatments, deworming and other routine tasks for each class of animal through the year. Your job is to plan the work so it happens on time.

Typical items on a calendar

  • Vaccinations, for example against clostridial diseases, anthrax, lumpy skin disease or brucellosis in heifers, as advised by your vet.
  • Tick and fly control by dipping, spraying or pour-ons, especially in summer.
  • Internal parasite control, ideally guided by faecal egg counts or FAMACHA scoring in sheep and goats, to slow resistance.
  • Hoof care, vitamin and mineral supplements and pregnancy testing.

Doing it properly

  1. Check that the right product is in stock, in date and stored as the label says (many vaccines need a fridge at 2–8 °C).
  2. Calculate doses from the label and the animals' weight. Do not guess. Never mix products unless the label allows it.
  3. Use clean, calibrated equipment and sterile needles. Change needles often.
  4. Handle animals calmly in a good crush. Protect workers with gloves and, where the label requires, overalls and eye protection.
  5. Record the date, product, batch number, dose, animals treated and withdrawal period.

Watch the animals daily

Train herders to notice early signs of disease: animals off feed, standing apart, lame, coughing, diarrhoea, drooling, sudden deaths. Sick animals must be separated into a sick pen and reported to the supervisor at once. Sudden unexplained deaths must not be opened up on the farm, because anthrax can infect people; call the vet.

lessons.title: Putting bio-security into practice
lessons.html:
Bio-security on the ground

Bio-security works only if everyone follows the rules every day. Write simple rules, put up signs and check that they are kept.

Keeping disease out

  • Isolate new animals in a separate camp for the period your vet advises, and test and treat them before they join the herd.
  • Control access – one entrance, a visitors' register, a gate kept closed, and parking for outside vehicles away from animal areas.
  • Footbaths and wheel dips – kept topped up with the correct disinfectant at the right strength; replace when dirty.
  • Clean clothing – farm overalls and boots for staff in poultry and pig houses.
  • Fences – maintained to keep out stray stock and wildlife.

Stopping spread inside the farm

  • Work from young and healthy animals to old and sick ones, never the other way.
  • Clean and disinfect pens, trailers and equipment after sick animals.
  • Dispose of carcasses quickly by approved methods, away from water sources.
  • Control rats, flies and wild birds around feed stores and houses.

Records and review

Keep the visitors' register, movement records, treatment register and mortality records. Review them monthly with the manager. Rising deaths or more sick animals in one camp tell you that something in the program is not working.

Key points

  • Bought-in animals, people, vehicles and wildlife are the main ways disease enters a farm.
  • Suspected notifiable diseases must be reported to the state veterinarian under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.
  • Follow the health calendar, the product label and your vet for doses and withdrawal periods.
  • Isolate new animals and control access with a register, footbaths and closed gates.
  • Never open a carcass after a sudden unexplained death; call the vet.
